newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Mid-Atlantic next-day power surges; Dec lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Mid-Atlantic next-day power surges; Dec lower.

text.p: Wholesale electricity prices for next-day delivery in the Mid-Atlantic U.S. surged Tuesday, extending Monday's gain tied to short-covering and higher heating demand due to winter-like temperatures.
"People are short-covering, and there is demand," said one Houston marketer.
Firm, peak electricity prices in the Mid-Atlantic were quoted midday in the $32.00-$34.00 a megawatt hour (MWh) range, sharply higher than Monday's $27.00-$28.00.
Hourly generation costs based on oil-fired generation in the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnect pool was assessed as high as $46.00 a megawatt hour (MWh), brokers and marketers said.
Market participants noted scheduling problem to move electricity to eastern and western PJM also contributed to today's jump in hourly and next-day prices.
Power scheduling into eastern PJM from the western district has been limited because of reduced operation at the Whitpain substation, north of Philadelphia.

Contrasting the rally in next-day prices, December PJM electricity for firm, peak delivery softened late morning after an early boost in tandem with a downturn in natural gas futures, brokers and marketers said.
December Henry Hub natgas futures were down 7.3 cents at $2.660 per million British thermal units after hitting a early high of $2.750.
December PJM deliveries were pegged at $28.40-$28.60, down from a quote of $28.50-$28.85 on Monday.
January/February 1997 PJM electricity was assessed at $32.40-$32.60, higher than Monday's $32.10-$32.50 range.
March 1997 PJM power was valued at $24.40-$24.80, up from $24.00-$24.60 on Monday.
The latest forecasts for Wednesday showed the Mid-Atlantic would experience peak temperatures in the 30s-40s Fahrenheit, and off-peak temperatures in the teens to 20s.
Extended outlook indicated the colder-than-normal weather in PJM would moderate next week.
